concepts: Definite integral of $\cos^2$ over whole periods
questions.question: If $\theta_1$ and $\theta_2$ are respectively the smallest and the largest values of $\theta$ in $(0,2\pi)-\{\pi\}$ which satisfy the equation $2\cot^2\theta-\frac{5}{\sin\theta}+4=0$, then $\int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2}\cos^2 3\theta\,d\theta$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Reduce the equation to a quadratic in $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$; then $\cos^2 3\theta$ is integrated by the double-angle formula.

alternate_solutions.idea: No antiderivative needed: the interval has length $\frac{2\pi}{3}$, exactly two periods of $\cos^2 3\theta$, so the integral is length $\times$ average value $\frac12$.
solution: As in the main solution, the equation gives $\sin\theta=\frac12$ and $\theta_1=\frac{\pi}{6}$, $\theta_2=\frac{5\pi}{6}$.
The interval $\left[\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}\right]$ has length $\frac{2\pi}{3}=2\cdot\frac{\pi}{3}$, i.e. exactly two full periods.
Over whole periods $\int\cos6\theta\,d\theta=0$, so the integral equals $\frac12\times$ length.

useful_results: Over a whole number of periods, $\int\cos^2(k\theta)\,d\theta=\int\sin^2(k\theta)\,d\theta=\frac12\times$ length (average value $\frac12$). Check: $\int_0^{\pi}\cos^2 2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}$.
$\cot^2\theta=\operatorname{cosec}^2\theta-1$ turns mixed $\cot$/$\operatorname{cosec}$ equations into a quadratic in one ratio; reject roots with $|\operatorname{cosec}\theta|<1$.

In this question $\operatorname{cosec}\theta=\frac12$ is rejected since $\sin\theta=2$ is impossible; the excluded point $\theta=\pi$ is where $\cot\theta$, $\operatorname{cosec}\theta$ are undefined.

questions.question: If $y=\left(\frac{2x}{\pi}-1\right)\operatorname{cosec}x$ is the solution of the differential equation $\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)\,y=\frac{2}{\pi}\operatorname{cosec}x$, $0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}$, then the function $p(x)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Differentiate the given solution and rewrite $\frac{dy}{dx}$ in the form $\frac{dy}{dx}+p\,y=\ldots$

alternate_solutions.idea: Substitute a convenient point: $p(x)=\dfrac{Q-y'}{y}$ at $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$ must match exactly one option.
solution: At $x=\frac{\pi}{6}$: $\tan x=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$, $\sec x=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$, $\cot x=\sqrt3$, $\operatorname{cosec}x=2$; only $\cot x$ equals $\sqrt3$, so $p(x)=\cot x$.

useful_results: If $y=u(x)\,e^{-\int p\,dx}$ then $y'+py=u'(x)\,e^{-\int p\,dx}$. Here $e^{-\int\cot x\,dx}=\operatorname{cosec}x$, so $p=\cot x$ and $u'=\frac2\pi$.
Given a solution of a linear first-order ODE, $p=\frac{Q-y'}{y}$ wherever $y\ne0$; a single test point usually separates the options.
Standard integrating factors: $\int\cot x\,dx=\ln|\sin x|$ gives I.F. $\sin x$; $\int\tan x\,dx=-\ln|\cos x|$ gives I.F. $\cos x$.

concepts: Definite integral of the greatest integer function
questions.question: The value of the integral $\int_1^3\left[x^2-2x-2\right]dx$, where $[x]$ denotes the greatest integer less than or equal to $x$, is:
questions.key_idea: Complete the square, $x^2-2x-2=(x-1)^2-3$; the $-3$ leaves the bracket, and $[t^2]$ is a step function.
useful_results: For an increasing $g\ge0$ on $[0,T]$: $\int_0^T[g(t)]\,dt=\sum_{k\ge1}\left(T-g^{-1}(k)\right)$ over the integers $k\le g(T)$ - one term per step instead of one integral per step.
$[x+n]=[x]+n$ for any integer $n$, so integer constants can be pulled out of the bracket before integrating.
Always complete the square first when the argument of $[\,\cdot\,]$ is a quadratic: the breakpoints are then $\sqrt{k}$ values around the vertex.

concepts: Definite integral of trigonometric functions using the $\tan x=t$ substitution
questions.question: The integral $\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\frac{dx}{\sin2x\left(\tan^5x+\cot^5x\right)}$ equals:
questions.key_idea: Write $\sin2x=2\sin x\cos x$ and $\tan^5x+\cot^5x=\frac{\tan^{10}x+1}{\tan^5x}$ to expose $\tan^4x\sec^2x\,dx$, then put $\tan^5x=U$.
solution: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos^2x$: $\sin x\cos x=\tan x\cos^2x$, so $=\frac12\int_{\pi/6}^{\pi/4}\frac{\tan^4x\sec^2x\,dx}{1+\tan^{10}x}$.
useful_results: $\int\frac{\tan^{n-1}x\sec^2x}{1+\tan^{2n}x}\,dx=\frac1n\tan^{-1}\left(\tan^nx\right)+C$: any $\frac{1}{\sin2x\,(\tan^nx+\cot^nx)}$ reduces to this, because $\frac{1}{\sin2x\,(\tan^n+\cot^n)}=\frac{\tan^{n-1}x\sec^2x}{2(1+\tan^{2n}x)}$.
$\tan^nx+\cot^nx=\frac{\tan^{2n}x+1}{\tan^nx}$ - rewrite sums of reciprocals as one fraction before substituting.
Check: $n=1$ gives $\int\frac{dx}{\sin2x(\tan x+\cot x)}=\int\frac{dx}{2}=\frac x2$, and the formula gives $\frac12\tan^{-1}(\tan x)=\frac x2$.
Limits transform as $t=\tan x$: $\tan\frac\pi6=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, $\tan\frac\pi4=1$; then $t^5$ at $\frac1{\sqrt3}$ is $\frac{1}{9\sqrt3}$.

concepts: Definite integral of trigonometric ratios ($\cot x$, $\operatorname{cosec}x$)
questions.question: If $\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cot x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}\,dx=m(\pi+n)$, then $m\cdot n$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\frac{\cot x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}=\frac{\cos x}{1+\cos x}=1-\frac{1}{1+\cos x}$, and $1+\cos x=2\cos^2\frac x2$.
solution: $\frac{\cot x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}=\frac{\cos x}{\cos x+1}$ (multiply numerator and denominator by $\sin x$).

alternate_solutions.idea: Weierstrass substitution $t=\tan\frac x2$ turns $\frac{\cos x}{1+\cos x}$ into a rational function with no half-angle manipulation.
solution: $\frac{\cot x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}=\frac{\cos x}{1+\cos x}$ as before.
Put $t=\tan\frac x2$: $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, $1+\cos x=\frac{2}{1+t^2}$, $dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$; limits $t=0$ to $1$.

useful_results: $\frac{\cot x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}=\frac{\cos x}{1+\cos x}$ and $\frac{\operatorname{cosec}x}{\cot x+\operatorname{cosec}x}=\frac{1}{1+\cos x}$ - convert everything to $\sin,\cos$ first.
$\frac{1}{1+\cos x}=\frac12\sec^2\frac x2$ and $\frac{1}{1-\cos x}=\frac12\operatorname{cosec}^2\frac x2$, with antiderivatives $\tan\frac x2$ and $-\cot\frac x2$.
$t=\tan\frac x2$ makes every rational function of $\sin x,\cos x$ rational in $t$; use it when nothing simpler works.

concepts: Area of the region bounded by modulus curves and a parabola
questions.question: The area (in sq. units) of the region $A=\{(x,y):|x|+|y|\le1,\ 2y^2\ge|x|\}$ is:
questions.key_idea: Both curves are symmetric in both axes, so find the first-quadrant area (square corner minus the parabola part) and multiply by 4.
solution: $|x|+|y|\le1$ is the square (diamond) with vertices $(\pm1,0),(0,\pm1)$; $2y^2\ge|x|$ is the region outside the parabolas $2y^2=x$ and $2y^2=-x$ (which open to the right and the left).
Both bounds are symmetric about both axes, so $A=4\times$ (area in the first quadrant).
In the first quadrant the parabola $x=2y^2$ meets $x+y=1$: $2y^2+y-1=0\Rightarrow y=\frac12$, $x=\frac12$, i.e. at $\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$.
First-quadrant triangle $x+y\le1$ has area $\frac12\cdot1\cdot1$; the region needed lies where $x\le2y^2$, i.e. above the curve $y=\sqrt{x/2}$.

So subtract the area under $y=\sqrt{x/2}$ for $0\le x\le\frac12$, which is $\int_0^{1/2}\sqrt{\frac x2}\,dx$, and the small triangle with vertices $\left(\frac12,0\right),(1,0),\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)$, of area $\frac12\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Slice horizontally: at height $y$ the allowed half-width is $\min(2y^2,\,1-|y|)$, so no square roots appear.
solution: By symmetry $A=4\times$ (first-quadrant area) $=4\int_0^1 m(y)\,dy$, where for each $y\in[0,1]$ the strip is $0\le x\le m(y)$ with $m(y)=\min\left(2y^2,\,1-y\right)$.
The two bounds cross at $2y^2=1-y$, i.e. $y=\frac12$; for $y<\frac12$, $2y^2<1-y$, and for $y>\frac12$, $1-y<2y^2$.

useful_results: When curves are of the form $x=f(y)$ (parabolas opening sideways), integrate with respect to $y$: it avoids square roots and the number of regions is often smaller.
Area of $|x|+|y|\le a$ is $2a^2$; the diamond has area $2$ here. Complement check: the part of the diamond with $2y^2<|x|$ has area $2-\frac56=\frac76$ (option (A) is that complement).
For regions symmetric in both axes, compute one quadrant and multiply by 4; always find the intersection points of the curves in that quadrant first.

questions.question: If $\int\frac{d\theta}{\cos^2\theta\left(\tan2\theta+\sec2\theta\right)}=\lambda\tan\theta+2\log_e|f(\theta)|+C$, where $C$ is a constant of integration, then the ordered pair $(\lambda,f(\theta))$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: $\tan2\theta+\sec2\theta=\frac{1+\sin2\theta}{\cos2\theta}=\frac{(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)^2}{(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)}$, which collapses to $\frac{1+\tan\theta}{1-\tan\theta}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Differentiate the candidate form and match it with the integrand: this fixes $\lambda$ and rules out each wrong option.
solution: The integrand simplifies to $\sec^2\theta\,\frac{1-t}{1+t}$ with $t=\tan\theta$ (as in the main solution, or using $\tan2\theta+\sec2\theta=\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\theta\right)=\frac{1+t}{1-t}$).
Equate to $\sec^2\theta\,\frac{1-t}{1+t}$: $\lambda(1+t)+2=1-t$ for all $t$, which forces $\lambda=-1$ (then $-1-t+2=1-t$).
For $f=1-\tan\theta$ the derivative is $\sec^2\theta\left[\lambda-\frac{2}{1-t}\right]=\sec^2\theta\,\frac{\lambda(1-t)-2}{1-t}$, whose denominator $1-t$ differs from $1+t$; no $\lambda$ works.

useful_results: $\tan2\theta+\sec2\theta=\frac{1+\sin2\theta}{\cos2\theta}=\tan\left(\frac\pi4+\theta\right)=\frac{1+\tan\theta}{1-\tan\theta}$; likewise $\sec2\theta-\tan2\theta=\frac{1-\tan\theta}{1+\tan\theta}$.
$1\pm\sin2\theta=(\cos\theta\pm\sin\theta)^2$ and $\cos2\theta=(\cos\theta-\sin\theta)(\cos\theta+\sin\theta)$.
$\int\frac{1-t}{1+t}\,dt=2\ln|1+t|-t+C$; in general divide first: $\frac{1-t}{1+t}=\frac{2}{1+t}-1$.
For an 'identify the form' question, differentiating the RHS and matching is a fast check of each option.

questions.question: The general solution of the differential equation $\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2+x^2y^2}+xy\frac{dy}{dx}=0$ is: (where $C$ is a constant of integration)
questions.key_idea: Factor $1+x^2+y^2+x^2y^2=(1+x^2)(1+y^2)$ to separate the variables, then use $1+x^2=t^2$ and $1+y^2=k^2$.
solution: Multiply and divide the left side by $x$: $\int\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}}{x^2}\,(x\,dx)=\int\frac{-y}{\sqrt{1+y^2}}\,dy$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Hyperbolic substitution $x=\sinh u$, $y=\sinh v$ makes $\sqrt{1+x^2}=\cosh u$ and the equation separates at sight.
solution: Put $x=\sinh u$, $y=\sinh v$: $\sqrt{1+x^2}=\cosh u$, $\sqrt{1+y^2}=\cosh v$, $dx=\cosh u\,du$, $dy=\cosh v\,dv$.
The equation $\sqrt{(1+x^2)(1+y^2)}\,dx=-xy\,dy$ becomes $\cosh u\cosh v\cosh u\,du=-\sinh u\sinh v\cosh v\,dv$.
Divide by $\sinh u\cosh v$: $\frac{\cosh^2u}{\sinh u}\,du=-\sinh v\,dv$, i.e. $\left(\sinh u+\frac{1}{\sinh u}\right)du=-\sinh v\,dv$.
Integrate: $\cosh u+\ln\tanh\frac u2=-\cosh v+C$, using $\int\frac{du}{\sinh u}=\ln\tanh\frac u2$.
$\tanh\frac u2=\frac{\cosh u-1}{\sinh u}=\sqrt{\frac{\cosh u-1}{\cosh u+1}}$, so $\ln\tanh\frac u2=\frac12\ln\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}+1}$.

useful_results: $1+x^2+y^2+x^2y^2=(1+x^2)(1+y^2)$ - spotting a product hidden in a sum is the usual way to separate variables.
For $\sqrt{1+x^2}$, either $x=\tan\theta$ or $x=\sinh u$ rationalises; $\int\frac{dx}{x\sqrt{1+x^2}}=\frac12\ln\left|\frac{\sqrt{1+x^2}-1}{\sqrt{1+x^2}+1}\right|+C$.
$\int\frac{dt}{t^2-1}=\frac12\ln\left|\frac{t-1}{t+1}\right|+C$; $\frac{t^2}{t^2-1}=1+\frac{1}{t^2-1}$ (divide before integrating).
Quick sign check on options: differentiating $\frac12\ln\frac{p+1}{p-1}$ ($p=\sqrt{1+x^2}$) gives $-\frac{1}{xp}$, matching the equation only for the $+$ combination in (A).

questions.question: If $\int\frac{dx}{\left(x^2-2x+10\right)^2}=A\left(\tan^{-1}\left(\frac{x-1}{3}\right)+\frac{f(x)}{x^2-2x+10}\right)+C$, where $C$ is a constant of integration, then:
questions.key_idea: Complete the square, $x^2-2x+10=(x-1)^2+9$, and put $x-1=3\tan\theta$ to get $\int\cos^2\theta\,d\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the standard reduction $\int\frac{du}{(u^2+a^2)^2}=\frac{1}{2a^2}\left[\frac{u}{u^2+a^2}+\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac ua\right]$, obtained from $\frac{d}{du}\frac{u}{u^2+a^2}$.

useful_results: $\int\frac{dx}{(x^2+a^2)^2}=\frac{1}{2a^2}\left[\frac{x}{x^2+a^2}+\frac1a\tan^{-1}\frac xa\right]+C$ (valid for $a\ne0$). Check: $a=1$, derivative of $\frac12\left[\frac{x}{x^2+1}+\tan^{-1}x\right]$ is $\frac{1}{(x^2+1)^2}$.
$x=a\tan\theta$ turns $\frac{1}{(x^2+a^2)^n}$ into $a^{1-2n}\cos^{2n-2}\theta\,d\theta$; and $\sin2\theta=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$ converts back.
Complete the square first: $x^2-2x+10=(x-1)^2+9$; shifting by $x-1$ first reduces the work.

questions.question: If $f(a+b+1-x)=f(x)$ for all $x$, where $a$ and $b$ are fixed positive real numbers, then $\frac{1}{a+b}\int_a^b x\left(f(x)+f(x+1)\right)dx$ is equal to:
questions.answer: (A) and (B) are both correct (each equals $\int_a^b f(x)\,dx$); the printed key (C) is wrong
questions.key_idea: Apply $x\to a+b-x$ and use $f(a+b-x)=f(x+1)$ to get a second expression; adding gives $\int_a^b\left(f(x)+f(x+1)\right)dx$.
solution: The given relation $f(a+b+1-x)=f(x)$ gives $f(a+b-x+1)=f(x)$, and (replacing $x$ by $x+1$) $f(a+b-x)=f(x+1)$.
Also $I=\int_a^bf(x)\,dx=\int_{a-1}^{b-1}f(x+1)\,dx$ (put $x=y+1$), which is option (A). Options (C) and (D) are not equal to $I$ in general.
questions.correction_note: The PDF ends with $I=\int_{a-1}^{b-1}f(x)\,dx$ (key C). That is wrong: $\int_a^bf(x+1)\,dx$ becomes $\int_{a+1}^{b+1}f(t)\,dt$ (limits shift by $+1$, not $-1$). Counter-example $f(x)=(x-2)^2$, $a=1$, $b=2$: $I=\frac13$, option (B) $=\frac13$, option (A) $=\frac13$, but option (C) $=\frac73$. Options (A) and (B) are both equal to $I$, so the question as printed has two correct options.

solution: So $g$ is symmetric about the midpoint $\frac{a+b}{2}$ of $[a,b]$; the 'centre of mass' of $x\,g(x)$ over $[a,b]$ is at $\frac{a+b}{2}$.

useful_results: If $g(a+b-x)=g(x)$ then $\int_a^bx\,g(x)\,dx=\frac{a+b}{2}\int_a^bg(x)\,dx$ (the weight $x$ can be replaced by its average $\frac{a+b}{2}$). Check: $g=1$ on $[0,2]$: $\int_0^2x\,dx=2=1\cdot2$.
$f(c+x)=f(c-x)$ means $f$ is symmetric about $x=c$; here $c=\frac{a+b+1}{2}$, so $\int_a^bf=\int_{a+1}^{b+1}f$ (reflection maps $[a,b]$ onto $[a+1,b+1]$).
Shifting limits: $\int_a^bf(x+k)\,dx=\int_{a+k}^{b+k}f(t)\,dt$ - the limits move the same way as the shift, not the opposite way.
When an answer key looks doubtful, test a symmetric function ($(x-c)^2$, $\cosh(x-c)$) on specific $a,b$; here it shows (C) is wrong.

questions.question: If $\int\left(e^{2x}+2e^x-e^{-x}-1\right)e^{\left(e^x+e^{-x}\right)}dx=g(x)\,e^{\left(e^x+e^{-x}\right)}+c$, where $c$ is a constant of integration, then $g(0)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Split the bracket as $\left(e^x-e^{-x}\right)+e^x\left(e^x-e^{-x}+1\right)$; each part is an exact derivative of $e^{h}$ for $h=e^x+e^{-x}$ or $h=e^x+e^{-x}+x$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes the second integrand as $\left(e^{2x}-e^{-x}-1\right)$; the correct remainder after removing $\left(e^x-e^{-x}\right)$ is $e^{2x}+e^x-1=e^x\left(e^x-e^{-x}+1\right)$. The later steps and the answer (A) 2 are right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Undetermined $g$: for $\int G\,e^{h}dx=g\,e^h$ we need $g'+g\,h'=G$; with $h'=e^x-e^{-x}$ try $g=e^x+c$.
solution: Matching with $e^{2x}+2e^x-e^{-x}-1$: coefficient of $e^x$ gives $1+c=2$, and of $e^{-x}$ gives $-c=-1$; both give $c=1$.

useful_results: $\int\left(g'+g\,h'\right)e^h\,dx=g\,e^h+C$: to find $g$, solve $g'+g\,h'=$ integrand$/e^h$ with a guess of the same 'shape' as the integrand.
$\frac{d}{dx}e^{h(x)}=h'(x)e^{h(x)}$; so $\int e^x\,e^{e^x}\,dx=e^{e^x}+C$ and generally $\int h'e^h=e^h$.
Absorb a factor into the exponent: $e^x\,e^{h}=e^{h+x}$, then $\frac{d}{dx}(h+x)=h'+1$ - this is how $e^x\left(e^x-e^{-x}+1\right)e^{h}$ becomes an exact derivative.
Check: $\frac{d}{dx}\left[(e^x+1)e^{e^x+e^{-x}}\right]=e^{e^x+e^{-x}}\left[e^{x}+(e^x+1)(e^x-e^{-x})\right]=\left(e^{2x}+2e^x-e^{-x}-1\right)e^{e^x+e^{-x}}$.

questions.question: Let $y=y(x)$ be the solution of the differential equation $\cos x\left(3\sin x+\cos x+3\right)dy=\left(1+y\sin x\left(3\sin x+\cos x+3\right)\right)dx$, $0\le x\le\frac\pi2$, $y(0)=0$. Then $y\left(\frac\pi3\right)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The equation is linear with integrating factor $\cos x$, leaving $\int\frac{dx}{3\sin x+\cos x+3}$, which the substitution $\tan\frac x2=t$ makes rational.
solution: Divide by $\cos x\,(3\sin x+\cos x+3)\,dx$: $\frac{dy}{dx}-y\tan x=\frac{1}{\cos x\,(3\sin x+\cos x+3)}$.
$y\cos x=\int\cos x\cdot\frac{dx}{\cos x\,(3\sin x+\cos x+3)}=\int\frac{dx}{3\sin x+\cos x+3}$.
useful_results: For $\frac{dy}{dx}+P\,y=Q$ the I.F. is $e^{\int P\,dx}$; for $P=-\tan x$ it is $\cos x$, and then $\frac{d}{dx}(y\cos x)=\cos x\cdot Q$.
Weierstrass: $\sin x=\frac{2t}{1+t^2}$, $\cos x=\frac{1-t^2}{1+t^2}$, $dx=\frac{2\,dt}{1+t^2}$, $t=\tan\frac x2$. Here it turns $3\sin x+\cos x+3$ into $\frac{2(t+1)(t+2)}{1+t^2}$.
Factorisation check: $3\sin x+\cos x+3=2\left(\cos\frac x2+\sin\frac x2\right)\left(2\cos\frac x2+\sin\frac x2\right)$.
$\int\frac{dt}{(t+a)(t+b)}=\frac{1}{b-a}\ln\left|\frac{t+a}{t+b}\right|+C$ ($a\ne b$); rationalise surds in the final value by multiplying by the conjugate.

concepts: Definite integral by substitution (rational function of $x$)
questions.question: The integral $16\int_1^2\frac{dx}{x^3\left(x^2+2\right)^2}$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Factor $x^4$ out of $x^3(x^2+2)^2$ to get $x^7\left(1+\frac2{x^2}\right)^2$, then put $t=1+\frac{2}{x^2}$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Put $u=x^2$ ($x\,dx=\frac{du}{2}$) and split $\frac{1}{u^2(u+2)^2}$ by partial fractions.

useful_results: For $\int\frac{dx}{x^{2k+1}(x^2+a)^m}$ put $u=x^2$ (odd power of $x$ gives $x\,dx=\frac{du}2$); for $\frac{1}{x^n(x^2+a)^m}$ with large $n$ the substitution $t=1+\frac{a}{x^2}$ also works.
$\frac{1}{u(u+a)}=\frac1a\left(\frac1u-\frac1{u+a}\right)$; squaring it gives the partial fractions of $\frac{1}{u^2(u+a)^2}$ at once.
After substitution, always convert the limits and re-check which limit is larger (here $t$ runs from $3$ down to $\frac32$, which supplies the minus sign).

concepts: Definite integral of the greatest integer function
questions.question: The value of $\int_0^{2\pi}\left[\sin2x\left(1+\cos3x\right)\right]dx$, where $[t]$ denotes the greatest integer function, is:
questions.key_idea: With $x\to2\pi-x$, $\sin2x(1+\cos3x)$ changes sign, and $[t]+[-t]=-1$ for non-integer $t$, so the two copies of the integral add to $-2\pi$.
solution: $[t]+[-t]=-1$ unless $t$ is an integer; $g$ is an integer only at isolated points, which do not affect the integral.

alternate_solutions.idea: Write $[g]=g-\{g\}$: the first part integrates to $0$ by odd symmetry about $\pi$, the fractional parts pair up to $1$.
solution: Let $g(x)=\sin2x\,(1+\cos3x)$. Then $g(2\pi-x)=-g(x)$, so $g$ is odd about $x=\pi$ and $\int_0^{2\pi}g\,dx=0$.

useful_results: $[t]+[-t]=-1$ for $t\notin\mathbb Z$ (and $=0$ for $t\in\mathbb Z$); $\{t\}+\{-t\}=1$ for $t\notin\mathbb Z$.
If $g(a-x)=-g(x)$ then $\int_0^a[g(x)]\,dx=-\frac a2$ (provided $g$ is non-integer almost everywhere); here $a=2\pi$ gives $-\pi$.
Do not try to find the breakpoints of $[\sin2x(1+\cos3x)]$ directly - it takes many pieces; look for a symmetry that makes pairs cancel.

Check with a simple case: $\int_0^{2\pi}[\sin x]\,dx$: $g=\sin x$ obeys $g(2\pi-x)=-g(x)$ and the formula gives $-\pi$ (direct: $\int_0^\pi0\,dx+\int_\pi^{2\pi}(-1)\,dx=-\pi$, ignoring the point $\frac\pi2$ where $[\sin x]=1$).

concepts: Area bounded by a closed curve (domain and symmetry)
questions.question: The area bounded by the curve $4y^2=x^2(4-x)(x-2)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: The curve exists only for $2\le x\le4$ and is symmetric about the $x$-axis; the area is $\int_2^4x\sqrt{(4-x)(x-2)}\,dx$, and $x\to6-x$ turns the weight $x$ into $3$.
solution: Upper branch $y_1=\frac x2\sqrt{(4-x)(x-2)}$; lower branch $y_2=-\frac x2\sqrt{(4-x)(x-2)}$.
$\int_2^4\sqrt{1-(x-3)^2}\,dx$ is the area of a semicircle of radius $1$, i.e. $\frac\pi2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Centroid view: $\int x\,h(x)\,dx=\bar x\cdot$ area, where $h=\sqrt{1-(x-3)^2}$ bounds a semicircle centred over $x=3$, so $\bar x=3$.
solution: The region $0\le y\le\sqrt{1-(x-3)^2}$ is a semicircle (area $\frac\pi2$) symmetric about the line $x=3$.
Hence the first moment $\int_2^4x\,h(x)\,dx=\bar x\times\text{area}=3\cdot\frac\pi2$, with $\bar x=3$ by symmetry.

useful_results: For $y^2=F(x)$ the curve is defined only where $F(x)\ge0$ and is symmetric about the $x$-axis; the area is $2\int\sqrt{F(x)}\,dx$ over those intervals.
$\int_{c-r}^{c+r}x\sqrt{r^2-(x-c)^2}\,dx=c\cdot\frac{\pi r^2}{2}$ (first moment of a semicircle, the odd part vanishes). Check: $c=3,r=1$ gives $\frac{3\pi}2$.
$(x-p)(q-x)=\left(\frac{q-p}2\right)^2-\left(x-\frac{p+q}{2}\right)^2$ - a product of two linear factors is a circle in disguise.

questions.question: The value of the integral $\int_0^1x\cot^{-1}\left(1-x^2+x^4\right)dx$ is:
questions.key_idea: Since $1-x^2+x^4>0$, $\cot^{-1}(\cdot)=\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{(\cdot)}$, and $\frac{1}{1+x^2(x^2-1)}$ is the difference form $\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ with $a=x^2$, $b=x^2-1$.
solution: First integral: put $x^2=t$, $2x\,dx=dt$; second: put $x^2-1=k$, $2x\,dx=dk$ (limits $k=-1$ to $0$).
questions.correction_note: The PDF's last lines are mis-typed: the second bracket is printed as $\left(-\frac\pi8-\frac14\ln2\right)$ followed by '$10-\ln2$'; the correct value of $\frac12\int_{-1}^{0}\tan^{-1}k\,dk$ is $-\frac\pi8+\frac14\ln2$, and subtracting it gives $\frac\pi4-\frac12\ln2$. The PDF's final answer (D) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Reflect $t\to1-t$ to see the two $\tan^{-1}$ pieces are equal, and get $\int_0^1\tan^{-1}t\,dt$ as an area using the inverse function.
solution: Area view: the region under $y=\tan^{-1}t$, $0\le t\le1$, and the region left of it up to $y=\frac\pi4$ together fill the rectangle $[0,1]\times\left[0,\frac\pi4\right]$.

useful_results: $\cot^{-1}z=\tan^{-1}\frac1z$ only for $z>0$ (for $z<0$ it differs by $\pi$); $1-x^2+x^4>0$ always, so it is safe here.

$\tan^{-1}a-\tan^{-1}b=\tan^{-1}\frac{a-b}{1+ab}$ when $ab>-1$; the denominator $1+x^2(x^2-1)$ is of the form $1+ab$ with $a=x^2$, $b=x^2-1$. Check: $x=1$: $\tan^{-1}1-\tan^{-1}0=\frac\pi4=\cot^{-1}1$.
$\int_0^1\tan^{-1}t\,dt=\frac\pi4-\frac12\ln2$ (and $\int_0^1f+\int_0^{f(1)}f^{-1}=1\cdot f(1)$ for an increasing $f$ with $f(0)=0$ - the area-of-inverse trick).
Telescoping patterns: $1+k(k+1)$, $1-x^2+x^4$ etc. in $\tan^{-1}$ arguments often signal the difference formula.

concepts: Determinant of a function and its derivative (Wronskian) $=0$
questions.question: Let $f$ be a twice differentiable function defined on $\mathbb R$ such that $f(0)=1$, $f'(0)=2$ and $f'(x)\ne0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. If $\begin{vmatrix}f(x)&f'(x)\\f'(x)&f''(x)\end{vmatrix}=0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$, then the value of $f(1)$ lies in the interval:
questions.key_idea: The determinant condition is $ff''-f'^2=0$, which is $\frac{d}{dx}\left(\frac{f'}{f}\right)=0$: so $f'=c\,f$.
solution: The determinant gives $f(x)f''(x)-\left(f'(x)\right)^2=0$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
$f$ is never $0$: if $f(x_0)=0$ the equation would force $f'(x_0)=0$, contradicting $f'\ne0$. So we may divide by $f^2$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Use the given $f'\ne0$ instead of $f\ne0$: divide $ff''=f'^2$ by $ff'$ to get $\frac{f''}{f'}=\frac{f'}{f}$.
solution: $f f''=f'^2$ and $f'\ne0$. Also $f\ne0$ (else $f'=0$ there), so divide by $f\,f'$: $\frac{f''}{f'}=\frac{f'}{f}$.
Thus $f\,e^{-2x}$ is constant, equal to its value $1$ at $x=0$; $f(x)=e^{2x}$ and $f(1)=e^2\in(6,9)$.

useful_results: $f f''-f'^2=0\iff\left(\ln f\right)''=0\iff f=a\,e^{kx}$ (when $f\ne0$); the determinant $\begin{vmatrix}f&f'\\f'&f''\end{vmatrix}$ is the Wronskian of $f$ and $f'$.
$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{f'}{f}=\frac{ff''-f'^2}{f^2}$ is the quotient-rule form to remember; $\frac{d}{dx}\frac{f}{f'}=\frac{f'^2-ff''}{f'^2}$ works the same way.
$f'=kf$ with $f(0)=A$ has the unique solution $f=Ae^{kx}$ (check $\left(fe^{-kx}\right)'=0$); here $k=2$, $A=1$.
Estimate $e^2\approx7.389$: remember $e\approx2.718$, $e^2\approx7.39$, $e^3\approx20.1$.

concepts: Indefinite integration of an irrational function by trigonometric substitution
questions.question: Let $f(x)=\int\frac{\sqrt x}{(1+x)^2}\,dx$ $(x\ge0)$. Then $f(3)-f(1)$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Put $\sqrt x=\tan\theta$: the integrand becomes $2\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Rationalise with $x=u^2$ and integrate by parts: $\int\frac{2u^2}{(1+u^2)^2}du=\int u\cdot\frac{2u}{(1+u^2)^2}du$.

useful_results: $\int\frac{\sqrt x}{(1+x)^2}\,dx=\tan^{-1}\sqrt x-\frac{\sqrt x}{1+x}+C$; more generally $\int\frac{dx}{(1+x^2)^2}$-type integrals come out as $\tan^{-1}$ plus a rational term.
$2\sin^2\theta=1-\cos2\theta$ and $\sin2\theta=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1+\tan^2\theta}$ convert back to $x$ quickly.
In $f(3)-f(1)$ the constant $C$ cancels - never carry it.
Check: derivative of $\tan^{-1}\sqrt x-\frac{\sqrt x}{1+x}$ is $\frac{1}{2\sqrt x(1+x)}-\frac{1-x}{2\sqrt x(1+x)^2}=\frac{\sqrt x}{(1+x)^2}$.

questions.question: Let $S(\alpha)=\{(x,y):y^2\le x,\ 0\le x\le\alpha\}$ and $A(\alpha)$ be the area of the region $S(\alpha)$. If for a $\lambda$, $0<\lambda<4$, $A(\lambda):A(4)=2:5$, then $\lambda$ equals:
questions.key_idea: $A(\lambda)=2\int_0^\lambda\sqrt x\,dx=\frac43\lambda^{3/2}$, so the ratio condition is $\left(\frac\lambda4\right)^{3/2}=\frac25$.
solution: $S(\lambda)$ is the part of $y^2\le x$ with $0\le x\le\lambda$: bounded by $y=\pm\sqrt x$ and the line $x=\lambda$.
questions.correction_note: The PDF writes $A(\lambda)=\frac43\lambda$ and $\frac{\lambda}{8}=\frac25$; the area is $\frac43\lambda^{3/2}$ and the equation is $\frac{\lambda^{3/2}}{8}=\frac25$ (the PDF then uses $\lambda=\left(\frac{16}{5}\right)^{2/3}$, which only follows from the correct equation). Answer (D) is right.

alternate_solutions.idea: Scaling: stretching $x$ by $s$ stretches $y$ by $\sqrt s$ on the family $y^2=x$, so the area scales as $s^{3/2}$.
solution: The region $S(\lambda)$ is the image of $S(4)$ under $(x,y)\to\left(\frac\lambda4x,\sqrt{\frac\lambda4}\,y\right)$, which maps $y^2=x$ to itself.

useful_results: Area of the segment of $y^2=4ax$ cut off by $x=h$ is $\frac83\sqrt a\,h^{3/2}$, i.e. two-thirds of the enclosing rectangle $h\times4\sqrt{ah}$. For $y^2=x$ ($a=\frac14$): $\frac43h^{3/2}$.
For $y^2=kx$ the area up to $x=\lambda$ is proportional to $\lambda^{3/2}$: ratio questions need only the exponent $\frac32$, never the constant.
$\left(\frac25\right)^{2/3}=\left(\frac4{25}\right)^{1/3}$; convert fractional powers into one cube root to match options.

questions.question: Let $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $\beta=\log_e(1-\alpha)$. Let $P_n(x)=x+\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^3}{3}+\dots+\frac{x^n}{n}$, $x\in(0,1)$. Then the integral $\int_0^\alpha\frac{t^{50}}{1-t}\,dt$ is equal to:
questions.key_idea: Write $t^{50}=\left(t^{50}-1\right)+1$ so that $\frac{t^{50}-1}{1-t}=-\left(1+t+\dots+t^{49}\right)$.

alternate_solutions.idea: Expand $\frac{1}{1-t}=\sum_{k\ge0}t^k$ and integrate term by term: the tail from $t^{50}$ onwards equals $-\ln(1-\alpha)$ minus the first 50 terms.

useful_results: $\int_0^\alpha\frac{t^n}{1-t}\,dt=-\ln(1-\alpha)-\sum_{k=1}^n\frac{\alpha^k}{k}$ for $\alpha\in(0,1)$ (division: $\frac{t^n}{1-t}=\frac{1}{1-t}-\left(1+t+\dots+t^{n-1}\right)$).
$-\ln(1-x)=x+\frac{x^2}2+\frac{x^3}3+\dots$ for $|x|<1$; so $P_n(x)$ is the $n$-th partial sum and $-\ln(1-x)-P_n(x)>0$ is its tail.
Geometric factorisation $1-t^n=(1-t)\left(1+t+\dots+t^{n-1}\right)$ is the key to any $\frac{t^n}{1-t}$ integral.
Sign check: the integrand is positive, so the answer must be positive: $-\beta=-\ln(1-\alpha)>P_{50}(\alpha)$, so $-\beta-P_{50}>0$ (option A), whereas (B) and (C) are negative for small $\alpha$.
